TheNewDetectives.us: Often, a killer will build the victim's trust before he or she attacks.
A corpse is found with a gunshot wound to the head; the weapon lies next to the victim.
Sometimes the faintest fingerprint or tire track is all investigators need to solve crimes.
A torso washes up on a river bank; a passer-by stumbles upon a human finger in a dumpster.
At a crime scene, anything left behind or moved out of place is considered a clue.
Forensic anthropologists use art and science to give faces to victims.
Sometimes arson fires are set to cover a different, more heinous crime, such as murder.
There's never a good reason for murder but some killers are especially cruel.
The great outdoors may offer clues to solving heinous crimes.
Some people do get away with murder, at least for a while.
In most murder cases, police rely on motive to pursue a killer.
When an unexpected crime occurs with no eyewitnesses, authorities must rely on forensic science.
The Texas Rangers, formed in the 1830s, evolve with the application of medical jurisprudence.
